extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO examiners, legislators, and policy advisors
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and explain substantive statutory and policy standards introduced or modified by the America Invents Act as discussed in the legislative commentary (definitions of prior art, effective filing date, fee authority, procedural options, and related doctrines). Useful for practitioners and policymakers needing the bill's operative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of fee-authority sources to avoid Origination Clause issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised language identifies with great specificity the sources of authority to impose patent and trademark user fees, in order to avoid a violation of the Origination Clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative text is drafted to enumerate the statutory sources giving the Director authority to set fees so as to remove any constitutional concern under the Origination Clause. No additional examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced fees for small entities for accelerated examination
rubrics_metrics.description: A new provision requiring the Director to charge reduced fees to small entities for use of accelerated examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy change mandates fee reductions specifically for small entities to access accelerated examination; intended to improve small-entity access to faster prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baldwin-rule repeal nonimplication for AOC obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is added making clear that the repeal of the Baldwin rule (which requires Federal Circuit judges to live within 50 miles of Washington, D.C.) shall not be construed to require the Administrative Office of the Courts (AOC) to provide judges office space or staff outside of D.C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that geographic residency change does not impose logistical/staffing obligations on the judiciary or AOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening of 'microentity' definition for reduced fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A PTO-approved broadening of the definition of 'microentity,' a status that entitles applicants to reduced fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expands eligibility for fee reductions; changes are PTO-approved and intended to increase access to reduced-fee status for qualifying applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax-patent carve-outs and clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In the tax patents section, language is added: (1) clarifying that the language does not bar patenting of tax software that is novel as software, and (2) establishing that making tax strategies unpatentable shall not be construed to imply that other business methods are patentable or valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twofold rule: prevents unintended blocking of patentable tax-related software; and clarifies that excluding tax strategies from patentability is not a general endorsement of business-method patentability. The commentary notes possible deletion of the software clause, so drafting may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: No derivative jurisdiction requirement for removal of patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Language added allowing removal of patent cases from state to federal court clarifies that derivative jurisdiction is not required in such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overrules/formally rejects the doctrine that a federal court's removal jurisdiction is derivative of the state court's jurisdiction; intended to avoid form-over-substance jurisdictional traps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schumer-Kyl business-method proceeding — limited standing
rubrics_metrics.description: Only defendants or accused infringers may invoke the Schumer-Kyl business-method proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrows who can initiate the administrative proceeding (defendants/accused infringers), limiting use and abuse by third parties or patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schumer-Kyl proceeding — prior-art limitation to old 102(a) public art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art in the Schumer-Kyl proceeding is limited to old 102(a), which must be publicly available, or prior art of old 102(a) scope that is presumed to beat old 102(a) invention-date limits but falls outside the old 102(b) grace period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts the universe of prior art that may be considered in the proceeding to publicly-available materials (narrower in some respects than broader prior-art pools), effectively excluding some newer or unpublished categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schumer-Kyl proceeding — cannot be used when PGR available
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeding may not be used to challenge a patent while it is eligible for a Post-Grant Review (PGR) challenge (i.e., an FTF patent during the first 9 months after its issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents concurrent or duplicative challenges; preserves priority of PGR during the initial post-issuance window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schumer-Kyl proceeding — four-year availability limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeding is available only for four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal limitation intended to limit prolonged administrative contesting of business-method patents and reduce litigation burden over older patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schumer-Kyl proceeding — stay decisions per Broadcast Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts decide whether to stay litigation based on the four-factor Broadcast Innovation test, and the Federal Circuit reviews stay decisions on interlocutory appeal to ensure consistent application of established precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates uniform stay-review framework: district courts apply Broadcast Innovation factors; Federal Circuit ensures consistent interlocutory review for predictable application across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of business-method patent narrowed to financial data-processing
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of business-method patent, which tracks the language of Class 705, is limited to data processing relating to just a financial product or service (rather than also to an enterprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrows scope of business-method patents to financial-product/service-related data processing; intended to reduce breadth of earlier Federal Circuit expansions like State Street.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO flexibility to pay and compensate APJ travel
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO is given greater flexibility in paying and compensating the travel of Administrative Patent Judges (APJs) to recruit, train, and retain the large number needed for PGR and new IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative/compensation change funded from existing funds to facilitate operational capacity for new post-grant mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: End fee diversion — PTO revolving fund (Coburn amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a revolving fund giving PTO direct access to its fees without the need for enactment of an appropriations act, ending fee diversion of PTO user fees to other federal spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural funding reform: PTO retains and uses collected fees directly through a revolving fund; intended to stabilize PTO financing and reduce dependence on annual appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of 'could have raised' and strong administrative estoppel rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection strengthened by inclusion of 'could have raised' estoppel, strong administrative estoppel, and explicit statutory authority for PTO to reject third-party petitions and order joinder of related parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory estoppel doctrines limit relitigation and manipulation of administrative processes; gives PTO authority to manage third-party petition filings and joinder for efficiency and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date definition clarified (actual filing date and incorporation of section 112/120 rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 100(i) definition modified: (A) the word 'actual' is added before 'filing date' to avoid ambiguity; (B) streamlined to clarify that a patent gets the benefit of an earlier application if it is entitled to such benefit or priority under the relevant code sections, which require satisfaction of section 112(a), a specific reference to the prior application, and copendency. The definition does not create new rules nor separately require enabling disclosure in the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition incorporates existing entitlement rules (including enabling disclosure requirement) by reference rather than restating them; avoids implying that enabling is unnecessary; precise phrasing avoids negative implications about entitlement to priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims added by amendment can be considered part of application for effective-filing-date purposes (no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent or application contains a claim to an invention even if the claim to the particular invention was added via an amendment after the application was filed, so long as such an amendment may not introduce new matter into the application—it may only claim that which was disclosed in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments are permissible to the extent they rely on original disclosure; introducing new matter remains barred and such additions would be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue treated as amendment; no new matter in reissue applications
rubrics_metrics.description: New section 100(i)(2) governs effective date of reissued patents: treats reissue as an amendment to the patent and bars introduction of new matter consistent with section 251 and section 132(a) (citing In re Rasmussen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissued patents are treated like amendments to pending applications; claims relying on new matter introduced in reissue are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recodification and reorganization of section 102 (consolidating exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 102 is recodified: exceptions to the definition of prior art consolidated into section 102(b); certain provisions that do not define exceptions (like CREATE Act and effective date definitions) are excluded from subsection (b). Wording changes made so parallel provisions operate in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational reform intended to eliminate misleading wording differences and make the statute's structure clearer; technical changes do not change substantive meaning except where noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor disclosure subparagraph (B) — first-to-publish effect in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 102(b)(1)(B) and 102(b)(2)(B), if an inventor publicly discloses his invention, no subsequent disclosure by anyone (or later-filed application by another) during the 1-year grace period will constitute prior art against that inventor's subsequent U.S. application; the inventor's earlier disclosure will still constitute prior art that invalidates others. The bill thus effectively creates a 'first to publish' rule guaranteeing U.S. patent rights to whoever discloses the invention to the public first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: public disclosure by an inventor preserves that inventor's U.S. rights against later filers/disclosers for one year. But such disclosure may forfeit overseas rights (Europe/Japan) unless a provisional or foreign filing strategy is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overseas filing caution — pre-filing disclosure prevents patenting abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's pre-filing disclosure will prevent patenting in Europe and Japan; an inventor concerned about foreign rights should file a provisional application in the United States to preserve both U.S. and overseas rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises prosecuting strategy: use provisional filings to avoid losing foreign patentability when disclosing publicly prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATE Act relocation and clarifying edits
rubrics_metrics.description: The CREATE Act is moved to section 102(c) with clarifying and technical changes: making the chapeau citation more specific, adding 'was developed' wording, replacing 'parties' with '1 or more parties', and moving the definition of 'joint research agreement' to section 100. Changes are intended to promote joint-research activities without altering original law's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/clarifying edits to better reflect intent and to avoid misinterpretation; no substantive change to the CREATE Act's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(d) changes and overruling remaining parts of In re Wertheim
rubrics_metrics.description: New subsection 102(d) modifies the effective date rules for patents and applications cited as prior art; paragraph (2) is intended to overrule remaining aspects of In re Wertheim by treating published applications (and provisional applications) as prior art as of their filing date even if they could not have become patents the day filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codifies contemporary BPAI and Federal Circuit practice (e.g., Ex parte Yamaguchi, Ex parte Robbins, In re Giacomini) that published applications and provisionals can be prior art as of their filing dates; reduces reliance on Wertheim's old technical requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for parent application to set effective prior-art date
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art parent application must be copendent, have some continuity of disclosure, and be specifically referred to in the patent or published application; continuous disclosure must describe the subject matter relied on as prior art (the disclosure can become narrower in intervening applications but must still exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (2) implements these requirements indirectly by requiring the prior application be 'entitled to claim priority or benefit' under section 120 et seq.; enables reliance on earlier fuller disclosures when continuity and specific reference are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: New section 102(a)(1) — public-availability and removal of geographic limits
rubrics_metrics.description: New section 102(a)(1) lifts current law's geographic limits on what uses, knowledge, or sales constitute prior art and limits all non-patent prior art to that which is available to the public (adding 'or otherwise available to the public').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The modifier 'or otherwise available to the public' is meant to restrict preceding clauses to publicly-available materials; consistent with committee report and judicial construction that such modifiers apply to preceding antecedent clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-accessibility standard for non-document disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A document is publicly accessible if it has been disseminated or otherwise made available such that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it and recognize and comprehend the essentials of the claimed invention without further research or experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote drawn from Cordis v. Boston Scientific; applies general accessibility test to both documents and non-document disclosures (e.g., products, public uses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of inherency applies to public-availability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under inherency, if an element is not expressly disclosed in a prior-art reference, the reference will still be deemed to anticipate a claim if the missing element is necessarily present in the thing described in the reference and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; applies to products sold to the public as well as published references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: once a product is sold on the market, any invention inherent to the product becomes publicly-available prior art and cannot be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of forfeiture doctrines in favor of general public-availability standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill eliminates patent forfeiture doctrines (current 102(b) on-sale and public-use bars) in favor of a general public-availability standard, reasoning that first-to-file incentives remove the need for strict forfeiture penalties and that forfeiture doctrines have produced harsh and arbitrary results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner's commentary criticizes cases (Beachcombers, JumpSport) where private, non-public uses triggered forfeiture; the new standard aims to avoid punishing secret sales/uses that do not make the invention accessible to the public.
